summary: Registers the application/xhtml+xml MIME media type for XHTML-based markup. It does not replace the text/html registration. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: XHTML is HTML rewritten in XML, so that a page can be checked for well-formedness and extended with new elements. Serving it under the ordinary HTML type does not tell the receiving software that it is XML. This memo registers a separate type for it, application/xhtml+xml, and sets out how such a file is recognised and how a link to a part of a page behaves.

subtitle: Registers the MIME type for XHTML pages, so that a receiver is told it is dealing with XML.

tldr.problem: XHTML 1.0 rewrote HTML in XML, but web pages of that kind were being served as text/html, which does not tell the receiving software that it is an XML processor.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers a new MIME media type, application/xhtml+xml, with an optional charset parameter and an optional profile parameter for content negotiation. It also says how a receiver can recognise such a file and how fragment identifiers behave.
tldr.outcome: It does not replace the text/html registration and it does not obsolete the document that registered it. It is Informational.

today: RFC 3236 is an Informational memo registering the application/xhtml+xml media type, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It says explicitly that it does not obsolete the registration of text/html, and that change control for the XHTML specifications lies with the W3C HTML Working Group. The XML Media Types document it builds on is RFC 3023.

sections.title: Why a New Media Type
sections.content:
In 1998 the W3C HTML working group began work on reformulating HTML in terms of XML 1.0 and XML Namespaces. The first part of that work concluded in January 2000 with the publication of the XHTML 1.0 Recommendation, the reformulation for HTML 4.01. Work continues in the Modularization of XHTML Recommendation, the decomposition of XHTML 1.0 into modules that can be used to compose new XHTML based languages, plus a framework for supporting that composition.

This document only registers a new MIME media type, application/xhtml+xml. It does not define anything more than is required to perform that registration, and it is not intended to obsolete any previous IETF document, in particular the document that registers text/html.

The memo follows the convention set out in the XML Media Types document for the MIME subtype name, attaching the suffix +xml to denote that the entity being described conforms to the XML syntax as defined in XML 1.0. It was prepared by members of the W3C HTML working group based on the structure, and some of the content, of the registration of text/html.
sections.plainLanguage: There was already a media type for HTML pages. This one says the same thing about a different flavour of HTML, and the memo is careful to say it adds to the older one rather than replacing it.

sections.title: The Registration
sections.content:
The registration is for the media type application with the subtype name xhtml+xml. There are no required parameters. Two optional parameters are defined. The charset parameter has identical semantics to the charset parameter of the application/xml media type. The profile parameter is described later in the memo.

On interoperability, XHTML 1.0 specifies user agent conformance rules that dictate behaviour which must be followed when dealing with, among other things, unrecognized elements. With respect to XHTML Modularization and the existence of XHTML based languages that are not XHTML 1.0 conformant, it is possible that application/xhtml+xml may be used to describe some of these documents. However, the memo says it should suffice for now that user agents accepting application/xhtml+xml content use the user agent conformance rules in XHTML 1.0.

Although conformant interpreters can expect that content received is well-formed XML, it cannot be guaranteed that the content is valid XHTML, in large part because of the previous paragraph. The published specification, XHTML 1.0, provides for describing some types of conformant content as text/html but does not disallow its use with other content types, which effectively allows for the possibility of this new type.

On the media type's use, the memo notes that some content authors have already begun hand and tool authoring on the Web with XHTML 1.0, but that this content is currently described as text/html, which allows existing web browsers to process it without reconfiguration for a new media type. There is no experimental, vendor specific or personal tree predecessor to application/xhtml+xml. The new type is being registered to allow for the expected deployment of XHTML on the World Wide Web as a first class XML application, where authors can expect that user agents are conformant XML 1.0 processors.

There is no single initial byte sequence always present in an XHTML file, but the memo gives guidelines for recognising them. There are three known file extensions in use for XHTML 1.0, .xht, .xhtml and .html. It is not recommended that the .xml extension be used, since web servers may be configured to distribute such content as text/xml or application/xml. The Macintosh file type code is TEXT, and the intended usage is COMMON. The XHTML specifications are a work product of the World Wide Web Consortium's HTML Working Group, and the W3C has change control over them.

Because XHTML content is XML, sending it as application/xhtml+xml has the same encoding considerations and the same charset default rules as XML.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration is short on purpose: a type name, two optional parameters, and a note that a receiver may assume the file is well-formed XML but not that it is valid XHTML. The rest is housekeeping, such as which file extensions are in use and who controls the specification.

sections.title: Fragment Identifiers
sections.content:
URI references may contain additional reference information identifying a certain portion of the resource. Such references end with a number sign followed by an identifier for that portion, called the fragment identifier, and the interpretation of fragment identifiers depends on the media type of the retrieval result.

For documents labelled as text/html, the registration of that type specified that the fragment identifier designates the correspondingly named element, identified by either a unique id attribute or a name attribute for some elements. For documents described with the application/xhtml+xml media type, fragment identifiers share the same syntax and semantics with other XML documents.

At the time of writing, the XML Media Types document does not define the syntax and semantics of fragment identifiers, but refers to the XML Pointer Language for a future XML fragment identification mechanism. Until that document is updated, fragment identifiers for XHTML documents designate the element with the corresponding ID attribute value, that is, any XHTML element with an id attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: When you follow a link to a named spot inside a page, the receiver works out which element you meant from the type of the page. For an XHTML page the rule is the XML one: the element whose id attribute matches the text after the number sign.

sections.title: Recognizing XHTML Files
sections.content:
All XHTML documents will have the string <html near the beginning of the document. Some will also begin with an XML declaration which begins with <?xml, though that alone does not indicate an XHTML document. All conforming XHTML 1.0 documents will include an XML document type declaration with the root element type html.

XHTML Modularization provides a naming convention by which a public identifier for an external subset in the document type declaration of a conforming document will contain the string //DTD XHTML. Some XHTML based languages require the doctype declaration to occur within documents of that type, such as XHTML 1.0 and XHTML Basic, but it is not the case that all XHTML based languages will include it.

All XHTML files should also include a declaration of the XHTML namespace. This should appear shortly after the string <html, and should read xmlns='http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml'.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no magic byte sequence for an XHTML file, so the memo lists the things to look for instead: the html tag near the top, a doctype naming html as the root element, and a declaration of the XHTML namespace just after the tag.

sections.title: The profile Parameter
sections.content:
The profile parameter is meant to solve the short-term problem of using MIME media type based content negotiation, such as the HTTP Accept header, to negotiate for a variety of XHTML based languages. It is intended to be used only during content negotiation, and it is not expected to be used to deliver content or that origin web servers have any knowledge of it, though they are welcome to. It is primarily targeted for use on the network by proxies in the HTTP chain that manipulate data formats, such as transcoders.

The parameter is intended to closely match the semantics of the profile attribute of the HEAD element as defined in HTML 4.01, except that it is applied to the document as a whole rather than just the META elements. The value of the profile attribute is a URI that can be used as a name to identify a language. The URI need not be resolved to be useful as a name, and it could be a namespace, a schema or a language specification.

The example the memo gives is that user agents supporting only XHTML Basic have no standard means to convey their inability to support the additional functionality in XHTML 1.0 that is not found in XHTML Basic. The XHTML Basic conformance rules, which are identical to XHTML 1.0, give some guidance, but the additional content in XHTML 1.0 that is not part of XHTML Basic is substantial, which makes those rules insufficient for practical processing and rendering to the end user. There is also the potentially substantial burden on the user agent in receiving and parsing that additional content.

The same functionality can be achieved with at least two other more general content description frameworks, the Content-features MIME header described in RFC 2912 and UAPROF from the WAPforum. Choosing one of these solutions would require excluding the other, because interoperability between the two has not been defined, so the memo suggests that this parameter be used until that issue is addressed. As part of an HTTP GET transaction the example is:

Accept: application/xhtml+xml; profile='http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml-basic/xhtml-basic10.dtd'
sections.plainLanguage: When a browser says which kinds of XHTML it can handle, this parameter lets it say which version. The value is a name, not a location, so nothing has to fetch it. The memo notes that two other frameworks could do the same job, but since they do not interoperate with each other it picked one for now.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The considerations for text/html and for application/xml also hold for application/xhtml+xml. In addition, because of the extensibility features for XHTML provided by XHTML Modularization, it is possible that application/xhtml+xml may describe content that has security implications beyond those described. However, if the user agent follows the user agent conformance rules in XHTML 1.0, that content will be ignored. Security issues could potentially arise only where the user agent recognizes and processes the additional content, or where further processing of that content is dispatched to other processors, and in that case they would fall outside the domain of this registration document.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual rules for HTML and for XML apply. The extra risk of modular XHTML comes from content a receiver does not recognise, and the memo's position is that a receiver following the XHTML rules will ignore such content anyway.

items.title: The html tag
items.text: Every XHTML document has an opening html tag near the beginning.

items.title: The XML declaration
items.text: Some files start with an XML declaration, but that alone does not identify an XHTML file.

items.title: The doctype
items.text: Every conforming XHTML 1.0 document has a document type declaration with html as the root element.

items.title: The namespace
items.text: A conforming file declares the XHTML namespace just after the html tag.
